<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hill-index" data-paper-title="Efficient Retrieval Scaling with Hierarchical Indexing for Large Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-hill-index-46d50ccf" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-b6cf5a4612015d03">Why involve user and interaction signals in HILL index-node training?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahill-index">Efficient Retrieval Scaling with Hierarchical Indexing for Large Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta / Facebook and Instagram Ads</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>ANN organizes item neighbors geometrically, which may disagree with complex relevance. Scoring pseudo-items with users transfers retrieval relations to the tree before narrowing candidates. Training, tree versions, and serving need to stay aligned.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two content neighbors with different audiences can be organized by recommendation value, not just item distance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12965">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2604.12965-hill-index/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b6cf5a4612015d03">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hill-index" data-paper-title="Efficient Retrieval Scaling with Hierarchical Indexing for Large Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-0781092bdcfe4d94">Why does HILL train index nodes with users and interaction towers instead of only clustering item vectors?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahill-index">Efficient Retrieval Scaling with Hierarchical Indexing for Large Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta / Facebook and Instagram Ads</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Pure item geometry may not match an interaction model&#x27;s choices. Train node proxies in user–item scoring and let deeper residuals recover information missed above. Beam search can still omit paths; isolated test answers cannot guide any test-time updates or selection.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Similar products may serve different users, so interaction-informed nodes can organize them better than content proximity alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12965">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2604.12965-hill-index/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0781092bdcfe4d94">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hill-index" data-paper-title="Efficient Retrieval Scaling with Hierarchical Indexing for Large Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-5406f6bb678f4cbe">Why can HILL residual layers complement each other instead of repeating raw-vector clustering?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahill-index">Efficient Retrieval Scaling with Hierarchical Indexing for Large Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta / Facebook and Instagram Ads</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each layer quantizes the prior layer&#x27;s unexplained residual, while repeated clustering can relearn dominant directions. Complementarity is not guaranteed and beam budgets can miss items. Local compression worked but quality regressed; fewer candidates are not automatically better.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After a coarse electronics node, residuals can express use and price rather than repeatedly learning the broad theme.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12965">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2604.12965-hill-index/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5406f6bb678f4cbe">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hill-index" data-paper-title="Efficient Retrieval Scaling with Hierarchical Indexing for Large Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-cbced8f5719b2196">Why validate HILL soft assignments and hierarchical beam separately?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahill-index">Efficient Retrieval Scaling with Hierarchical Indexing for Large Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta / Facebook and Instagram Ads</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Continuous training assignments create pseudo-items and gradients; serving explores a limited discrete tree. Check normalization, residual updates, parent-child mapping, and actual budgets independently, including small-catalog variance. Good reconstruction does not establish beam coverage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A target can receive small mass from several soft nodes and be absent from every retained hard branch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12965">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2604.12965-hill-index/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cbced8f5719b2196">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:llm-ad-retrieval" data-paper-title="LLM Retrieval for Stable and Predictable Ad Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-llm-ad-retrieval-68e38a71" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ec68ff836f180cae">Why must an A/A′ shadow-ad perturbation preserve ad meaning?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Allm-ad-retrieval">LLM Retrieval for Stable and Predictable Ad Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It tests stability to irrelevant changes. Meaningful edits can reasonably change distribution. Alter formatting or equivalent wording to probe reliance on IDs or superficial sparse features. Stability is distinct from relevance: identical wrong retrieval is stable too.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Punctuation and equivalent year formats should largely preserve audience; replacing children&#x27;s shoes with hiking boots genuinely changes the product.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21969">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.21969-llm-ad-retrieval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ec68ff836f180cae">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:llm-ad-retrieval" data-paper-title="LLM Retrieval for Stable and Predictable Ad Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a8d03d3e65df1df8">Why add A/A′ predictability checks to LLM ad retrieval instead of only measuring Recall?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Allm-ad-retrieval">LLM Retrieval for Stable and Predictable Ad Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Small edits preserving creative semantics can still change delivery sharply through IDs and sparse signals, without showing up in Recall. A primary/shadow pair measures conversion and exposure drift; hierarchical semantic attributes and an ad graph offer transferable connections. Control sampling noise before declaring a small difference a failure.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Rephrasing an ad without changing its meaning can nearly erase its impressions while standard hit rates remain good. A paired shadow ad specifically tests such sensitivity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21969">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.21969-llm-ad-retrieval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a8d03d3e65df1df8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:llm-ad-retrieval" data-paper-title="LLM Retrieval for Stable and Predictable Ad Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-14f5757cdd50ff78">What does an LLM semantic graph add for new ads and stability compared with a collaborative item graph?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Allm-ad-retrieval">LLM Retrieval for Stable and Predictable Ad Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Collaborative edges come from co-consumption. Semantic attributes connect behavior-sparse creatives and can reduce drift under meaningless rewrites. Hallucinations require confidence and expansion budgets. The local result is a fixed-budget routing increment, not end-to-end ad effectiveness or strong evidence about training variance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: An ad with no co-click edge can connect by brand and use. A misidentified brand can also expand to wrong candidates, so more edges alone are not better.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21969">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.21969-llm-ad-retrieval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-14f5757cdd50ff78">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:llm-ad-retrieval" data-paper-title="LLM Retrieval for Stable and Predictable Ad Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-3159eea7b4ec5c7a">Why don&#x27;t three identical tie-breaking seeds prove zero training variance in local LLM ad retrieval?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Allm-ad-retrieval">LLM Retrieval for Stable and Predictable Ad Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The model was not independently retrained for each seed, and there were no score ties to break. Identical results establish deterministic postprocessing only. Report A/A′ attribute and score drift separately from Recall and NDCG.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Changing the tie-breaking seed for one checkpoint on a list with no ties naturally produces the same list, not three independently stable training results.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21969">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.21969-llm-ad-retrieval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3159eea7b4ec5c7a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mdcns" data-paper-title="Divergence Meets Consensus: A Multi-Source Negative Sampling Framework for Sequential Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-mdcns-8e8ced60" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7c4b021a66342a05">Why does MDCNS use Self, Peer, and Teacher for negatives?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amdcns">Divergence Meets Consensus: A Multi-Source Negative Sampling Framework for Sequential Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 论文作者团队（原文未标注公司）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One model&#x27;s high score can reflect bias or a true unlabeled positive. Peer provides a heterogeneous judgment, Teacher aggregates both, and disagreement identifies hard informative items. False negatives remain possible; distillation over the pool conveys relations a single selected negative misses.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Self and Peer can disagree about a camera&#x27;s relevance. A missing interaction does not show the user dislikes it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19651">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.19651-mdcns/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7c4b021a66342a05">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mdcns" data-paper-title="Divergence Meets Consensus: A Multi-Source Negative Sampling Framework for Sequential Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-451af1c0d313f3a2">Why consider Self–Peer disagreement in MDCNS rather than always choosing Self&#x27;s highest-scoring negative?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amdcns">Divergence Meets Consensus: A Multi-Source Negative Sampling Framework for Sequential Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 论文作者团队（原文未标注公司）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A high Self score may be bias or an unlabeled positive; repeatedly choosing it reduces diversity. A heterogeneous Peer adds another view, disagreement finds informative candidates, and Teacher distills relationships across the full pool to Self. Disagreement does not establish a negative label; manage false negatives and training stability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: If Self over-scores popular items and Peer disagrees, the discrepancy reveals uncertainty, not proof that every disputed item is irrelevant.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19651">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.19651-mdcns/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-451af1c0d313f3a2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mdcns" data-paper-title="Divergence Meets Consensus: A Multi-Source Negative Sampling Framework for Sequential Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-1cc07ab0f592c36a">Why sample randomly from top M in MDCNS instead of DNS&#x27;s fixed highest-score choice?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amdcns">Divergence Meets Consensus: A Multi-Source Negative Sampling Framework for Sequential Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 论文作者团队（原文未标注公司）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Always taking the hardest candidate can repeatedly chase one outlier or false negative. Sampling within top M broadens hard-region coverage. Disagreement reranking and multiple losses reduce dependence on one model but still depend on pool quality. The small Markov backbone supports the sampling result only, not large sequence-model reproduction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: If one popular film always tops the negatives, sampling among five hard items avoids centering every update on that suspected false negative.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19651">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.19651-mdcns/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1cc07ab0f592c36a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mdcns" data-paper-title="Divergence Meets Consensus: A Multi-Source Negative Sampling Framework for Sequential Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-55b0814cd9fac24b">Why compute MDCNS Teacher KL over the whole pool instead of the chosen negative alone?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amdcns">Divergence Meets Consensus: A Multi-Source Negative Sampling Framework for Sequential Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 论文作者团队（原文未标注公司）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One negative supplies a local pair; the full Teacher distribution conveys relative difficulty across candidates. Align Self/Peer columns by identity and preserve temperature and τ² scaling. Build unobserved candidates at the training cutoff rather than using test answers to filter them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Even if one pair is sampled from 30 candidates, KL can convey which of the other 29 are close. A single scalar normalized to one contains no distributional knowledge.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19651">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.19651-mdcns/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-55b0814cd9fac24b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:melo" data-paper-title="Melo: A Production LLM-Powered Music Recommendation Agent" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-melo-f661791b" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d38970c261e7939e">Why split Melo into intent, retrieval, recommendation, and explanation nodes?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amelo">Melo: A Production LLM-Powered Music Recommendation Agent</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NetEase Cloud Music / Zhejiang University of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each has distinct inputs and failure conditions. Grounding maps generated entities to available items, and feedback decides whether reflection is needed. Staging makes repair traceable. A legitimate entity need not be relevant, and a fluent explanation cannot fix a wrong candidate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Repair mapping for an invented film title before explaining it; if a real film is irrelevant, inspect intent or retrieval.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23718">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.23718-melo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d38970c261e7939e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:melo" data-paper-title="Melo: A Production LLM-Powered Music Recommendation Agent" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-8e338a94d4aae060">Why does Melo ground entities after recommendation and reflect before retrying failures?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amelo">Melo: A Production LLM-Powered Music Recommendation Agent</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NetEase Cloud Music / Zhejiang University of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fluent music descriptions can name nonexistent or mismatched entities. Grounding validates outputs against the real catalog before returning them. Reflection uses the failure to revise intent or retrieval rather than arbitrarily regenerating. Catalog validity and preference quality need separate measures.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: If a plausible song is absent from the catalog, revisit intent and retrieval instead of forcing a near match or treating any valid song as relevant.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23718">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.23718-melo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8e338a94d4aae060">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:melo" data-paper-title="Melo: A Production LLM-Powered Music Recommendation Agent" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b4aaf679737868f4">How does one reflective retry in Melo trade reliability against unbounded generation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amelo">Melo: A Production LLM-Powered Music Recommendation Agent</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NetEase Cloud Music / Zhejiang University of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A bounded retry can repair grounding while controlling cost. Repeated generation can hallucinate again or eventually guess by luck. Trigger on catalog validity and confidence, then assess repaired quality independently. The local freshness increase came with overall regression, so repairs alone do not prove improvement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Check the catalog and retry a bad film name once. Repeating until any answer matches inflates success and latency.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23718">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.23718-melo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b4aaf679737868f4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:melo" data-paper-title="Melo: A Production LLM-Powered Music Recommendation Agent" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-a7d0077c574dea15">Why does Melo need a threshold and failure state even if post-grounding argmax always yields a valid entity?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amelo">Melo: A Production LLM-Powered Music Recommendation Agent</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NetEase Cloud Music / Zhejiang University of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Argmax returns some catalog ID even if every score is low. Thresholds detect insufficient evidence, and original entity validity must be logged before mapping. Checking only whether the mapped result exists hides hallucinations. The local path permits one defined retry.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: An invented title can map to a real but unrelated movie. Catalog membership after mapping alone misses the error.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23718">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.23718-melo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a7d0077c574dea15">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mesh" data-paper-title="MESH: Scaling Up Retrieval with Heterogeneous Content Unification" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-mesh-881b1237" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7c782c1ba17874b8">Why scale inside the user, item, and context sub-towers first in MESH?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amesh">MESH: Scaling Up Retrieval with Heterogeneous Content Unification</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Flat interaction can let frequent evergreen signals dominate gradients. Separate cross interactions retain structure before a context gate adjusts affinity. The aim is more balanced capacity use, not guaranteed fresh/tail gains; inspect cohort and aggregate metrics.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Encode stable preferences, item freshness, and request context separately so popular-item statistics do not drown out context from the start.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12392">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.12392-mesh/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7c782c1ba17874b8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mesh" data-paper-title="MESH: Scaling Up Retrieval with Heterogeneous Content Unification" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-23bf7dbdc9d448ab">Why scale user, item, and context sub-towers separately in MESH before global interaction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amesh">MESH: Scaling Up Retrieval with Heterogeneous Content Unification</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Flattening early lets strong common-item gradients obscure fresh and tail signals. Residual cross interactions within each sub-tower retain specialized capacity; a context gate then adjusts user–item affinity per request. A cacheable item tower does not remove candidate-dependent scoring costs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Model a tail item&#x27;s content before it competes with popular exposure counts, then judge the item in the request context.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12392">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.12392-mesh/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-23bf7dbdc9d448ab">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mesh" data-paper-title="MESH: Scaling Up Retrieval with Heterogeneous Content Unification" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-323fdf049a2e98cf">When can MESH&#x27;s parallel towers be faster than a flat serial model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amesh">MESH: Scaling Up Retrieval with Heterogeneous Content Unification</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Independent towers permit concurrency and async item caching, but speed depends on runtime, hardware, batch size, and synchronization. A parallelizable graph is not necessarily executed in parallel by small-batch Python. The local slowdown is valid evidence. Compare quality and compute separately instead of inferring throughput from tower count.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Three towers run sequentially in one CPU loop with no GPU concurrency and more scheduling overhead; they do not become three times faster by design alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12392">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.12392-mesh/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-323fdf049a2e98cf">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mesh" data-paper-title="MESH: Scaling Up Retrieval with Heterogeneous Content Unification" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-296affeb40c412ba">Why does RGBC gate elementwise user–item affinity with context and add a context residual?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amesh">MESH: Scaling Up Retrieval with Heterogeneous Content Unification</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The product models corresponding dimensions of user and item vectors. A sigmoid context gate selects affinities useful now, while the residual retains context itself. Align dimensions and identity across towers. Averaging context loses sample conditioning, and layer-normalization and residual placement matter.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Commuting and weekend contexts can emphasize different affinity dimensions for the same pair, while context independently represents time. A final constant bias cannot do this.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12392">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.12392-mesh/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-296affeb40c412ba">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mfli" data-paper-title="Rethinking ANN-based Retrieval: Multifaceted Learnable Index for Large-scale Recommendation System" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-mfli-7f2af977" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c0622b3380a540c5">Why learn a retrieval index in MFLI rather than build ANN on existing vectors?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amfli">Rethinking ANN-based Retrieval: Multifaceted Learnable Index for Large-scale Recommendation System</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Independent ANN organizes geometric neighbors; multiple objectives share one space and updates can lag. Learned facets organize semantics, popularity, and time differently and allocate request-dependent budgets. Task linkage does not eliminate update cost or coverage issues.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: An item can occupy separate semantic and freshness facets, and the request decides which to search more.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16124">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2602.16124-mfli/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c0622b3380a540c5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mfli" data-paper-title="Rethinking ANN-based Retrieval: Multifaceted Learnable Index for Large-scale Recommendation System" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-75db5ab44a747faf">Why learn the index in MFLI and allocate retrieval budget per request and facet?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amfli">Rethinking ANN-based Retrieval: Multifaceted Learnable Index for Large-scale Recommendation System</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One geometry struggles to represent semantics, popularity, and freshness, and an offline index can lag the model. Learned facets preserve distinct structures, and each request allocates candidate quotas among them. Maintain coverage and update consistency; removing traditional ANN does not automatically improve quality and cost.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Exploration can favor freshness, while an exact category can favor semantics. Equal quotas on every request do not exploit context.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16124">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2602.16124-mfli/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-75db5ab44a747faf">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mfli" data-paper-title="Rethinking ANN-based Retrieval: Multifaceted Learnable Index for Large-scale Recommendation System" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-33f382dac78ac62b">How does MFLI allocate budgets differently from concatenating multiple retrieval outputs?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amfli">Rethinking ANN-based Retrieval: Multifaceted Learnable Index for Large-scale Recommendation System</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It jointly designs learned facets and request weights a(q), which affect resource allocation. Simple concatenation can use fixed quotas and unrelated spaces. Learned facets do not guarantee less popularity bias: local head share increased, so inspect the actual distribution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Search freshness more for new products and semantics more for a specific model. Ten from each branch for every request can duplicate popular items.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16124">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2602.16124-mfli/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-33f382dac78ac62b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mfli" data-paper-title="Rethinking ANN-based Retrieval: Multifaceted Learnable Index for Large-scale Recommendation System" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-305b55efe709b3f3">Why verify MFLI facet softmax and actual candidate quotas separately?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amfli">Rethinking ANN-based Retrieval: Multifaceted Learnable Index for Large-scale Recommendation System</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Weights summing to one do not establish correct integer allocation. Rounding, total budget, and empty facets matter. Map code identities back to items and deduplicate. The four-facet local proxy does not measure industrial refresh or throughput.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Rounding three equal shares of a ten-item budget yields only nine; define where the remainder goes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16124">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2602.16124-mfli/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-305b55efe709b3f3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mima" data-paper-title="MIMA: Multi-Interest Recommendation via Multi-Positive Exclusive Assignment" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-mima-5191fe9f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-1132beb05c6cad64">Why treat positives in one MIMA request as a set rather than imposing an order?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amima">MIMA: Multi-Interest Recommendation via Multi-Positive Exclusive Assignment</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Coexisting interests need not be assigned by artificial order. Set matching is permutation-insensitive and encourages specialization; routing estimates actual activation. Historical encoding can still be causal; only positive supervision changes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A request can like shoes and a pack without defining which to learn first or letting the strongest sports channel explain both.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12842">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.12842-mima/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1132beb05c6cad64">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mima" data-paper-title="MIMA: Multi-Interest Recommendation via Multi-Positive Exclusive Assignment" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a7737838b5685202">Why match multiple positives in a MIMA request one-to-one with interests instead of independently choosing the closest?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amima">MIMA: Multi-Interest Recommendation via Multi-Positive Exclusive Assignment</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Independent selection can send all gradients to one interest. MIMA forms an interest–positive similarity cost matrix and finds a globally optimal one-to-one assignment, giving distinct interests supervision. Activation probabilities then calibrate channels. Specialization comes from set supervision, not just more vectors.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Running shoes and a hiking pack can both choose one sports channel under independent matching. A one-to-one assignment makes two channels explain the positives separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12842">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.12842-mima/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a7737838b5685202">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mima" data-paper-title="MIMA: Multi-Interest Recommendation via Multi-Positive Exclusive Assignment" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-34e97c32a3372408">How does one-to-one MIMA matching avoid crowding one channel compared with independently taking the nearest interest?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amima">MIMA: Multi-Interest Recommendation via Multi-Positive Exclusive Assignment</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Independent argmax can give all positives to one interest and starve the others. Global assignment distributes slots to minimize total cost. Define unmatched handling when counts differ; forced matching can also give a noisy positive its own channel and does not ensure semantic independence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Two items slightly prefer interest one. One-to-one matching evaluates the total cost of assigning either to interest two, unlike greedy independent matching.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12842">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.12842-mima/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-34e97c32a3372408">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mima" data-paper-title="MIMA: Multi-Interest Recommendation via Multi-Positive Exclusive Assignment" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-8833e9be64e7f356">When do exhaustive search and Hungarian matching optimize the same MIMA objective, and what cannot replace them?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amima">MIMA: Multi-Interest Recommendation via Multi-Positive Exclusive Assignment</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Both solve the same cost matrix&#x27;s optimal one-to-one assignment; exhaustive search can verify small cases. Greedy matching is generally not equivalent. Use aligned interest–positive similarities and separately calibrate channels with log activation probability. Plausible pairs do not establish optimality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A greedy first positive can take the only good slot for the second. Exhaustive enumeration can find the lower-cost allocation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12842">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.12842-mima/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8833e9be64e7f356">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mpformer" data-paper-title="MPFormer: Adaptive Framework for Industrial Multi-Task Personalized Sequential Retriever" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-mpformer-268b1045" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-3da58df8da20b61e">Why use objective tokens for MPFormer retrieval goals?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ampformer">MPFormer: Adaptive Framework for Industrial Multi-Task Personalized Sequential Retriever</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Different feedback goals need different views of the same history. An objective token conditions a shared backbone, and task difficulty informs capacity and candidate allocation. A token is an interface, not supervision; renaming it cannot teach an unsupported behavior.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A user may click novel items and purchase trusted ones. Training only on views does not teach purchasing by swapping the objective token.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.20400">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2508.20400-mpformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3da58df8da20b61e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mpformer" data-paper-title="MPFormer: Adaptive Framework for Industrial Multi-Task Personalized Sequential Retriever" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-76a6ff70ef5af788">How does MPFormer&#x27;s objective token produce retrieval representations for different goals from the same history?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ampformer">MPFormer: Adaptive Framework for Industrial Multi-Task Personalized Sequential Retriever</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The objective token conditions the sequence encoder, so shared layers can extract different signals for different behavior goals. Dynamic weights and quotas adjust learning and retrieval budgets by difficulty. Calibrate goals separately; they are not interchangeable next-item targets.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Click retrieval can favor novelty while purchase retrieval emphasizes recent repeated comparisons, changing both features and candidate quota.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.20400">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2508.20400-mpformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-76a6ff70ef5af788">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mpformer" data-paper-title="MPFormer: Adaptive Framework for Industrial Multi-Task Personalized Sequential Retriever" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-3e14785dbbaeabdb">How do MPFormer dynamic quotas change serving budgets relative to fixed K per task?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ampformer">MPFormer: Adaptive Framework for Industrial Multi-Task Personalized Sequential Retriever</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Dynamic quotas allocate by difficulty or context, potentially increasing coverage for hard goals while crowding out others. Normalized weights do not ensure valid integer budgets. The public proxy does not establish gains for every industrial behavior objective.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Allocate less to easy click retrieval and more to sparse purchases, unless the difficulty estimate misallocates the extra capacity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.20400">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2508.20400-mpformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3e14785dbbaeabdb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mpformer" data-paper-title="MPFormer: Adaptive Framework for Industrial Multi-Task Personalized Sequential Retriever" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-fab82113a426caac">Why record how MPFormer&#x27;s qm(h) is used for training weights versus candidate quotas?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ampformer">MPFormer: Adaptive Framework for Industrial Multi-Task Personalized Sequential Retriever</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Normalized continuous weights multiply losses; serving counts need integer conversion and a total cap. Mask missing labels instead of making up zero supervision. Mixing proxy scores does not train an objective-conditioned shared model.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A training weight of 0.3 does not automatically mean 30 candidates; with total budget ten, define rounding and remainder.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:muser" data-paper-title="MuSeR: Scalable Long-sequence Recommendation with Multi-interest Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">

<span id="paper-recommendation-muser-f887e208" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-8ffaaf0436b17c9f">Why use an orthogonality regularizer for MuSeR&#x27;s learned interest queries?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amuser">MuSeR: Scalable Long-sequence Recommendation with Multi-interest Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Baidu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Several queries may all read the same popular pattern. Penalizing similar interest directions encourages specialization for candidate selection. Geometry does not ensure semantic complementarity and can separate genuinely related interests. Use ablations and task metrics.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Distinct photography and camping queries can help coverage, but random orthogonal vectors are not useful by themselves.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

</details>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:muser" data-paper-title="MuSeR: Scalable Long-sequence Recommendation with Multi-interest Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-96e91ee29d96d6b7">Why compress recent, medium, and distant history at different strides and let candidates choose MuSeR interests?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amuser">MuSeR: Scalable Long-sequence Recommendation with Multi-interest Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Baidu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Detailed recent events preserve immediate intent; larger distant strides control cost. Learned queries extract multiple interests, and candidate similarity selects a mixture. Compression determines how much history to read; candidate conditioning determines what to use. Pooling can still lose rare old events.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Summarize long-running photography and retain each recent camping view. A camera and tent activate different interests.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23677">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.23677-muser/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-96e91ee29d96d6b7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:muser" data-paper-title="MuSeR: Scalable Long-sequence Recommendation with Multi-interest Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-da9523e9a8606b73">What conditioning does MuSeR preserve by selecting interests per candidate instead of averaging?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amuser">MuSeR: Scalable Long-sequence Recommendation with Multi-interest Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Baidu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A common mean gives every item the same summary. Candidate softmax reads different interests according to similarity, requiring candidate-specific weights rather than wholly shared cache state. Local label fusion is not the full ERNIE/BGE multimodal pipeline.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Cameras emphasize photography and tents emphasize camping; averaging weakens each relevant signal.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23677">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.23677-muser/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-da9523e9a8606b73">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:muser" data-paper-title="MuSeR: Scalable Long-sequence Recommendation with Multi-interest Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-68f338a526b6f67a">Why report absolute scores and component results alongside large relative local MuSeR Recall gains?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amuser">MuSeR: Scalable Long-sequence Recommendation with Multi-interest Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Baidu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A low baseline makes small absolute changes look large in percentage terms. The hierarchical compression ablation was small, so do not credit it with the joint gain. State user sampling and full-catalog scope; label proxies do not establish original LLM summary gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Recall from 1% to about 2.6% looks large relatively, but most targets still miss the top ten.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

</details>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:next-vlm" data-paper-title="NEXT: Reasoning-Driven Video Recommendation via a Vision-Language Model" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
