<span id="paper-recommendation-next-vlm-e4f6498d" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f372a46478cadf88">Why can&#x27;t NEXT automatically reverse every directed edge?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Anext-vlm">NEXT: Reasoning-Driven Video Recommendation via a Vision-Language Model</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A need after A need not reverse after B. Explicit sequels and inferred needs both create directional relations; serving triggers confident edges after positive engagement. Inferred transitions are not observed consumption.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: An unboxing can lead to an extraction tutorial without the tutorial leading back to an unboxing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24789">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.24789-next-vlm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f372a46478cadf88">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:next-vlm" data-paper-title="NEXT: Reasoning-Driven Video Recommendation via a Vision-Language Model" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-7f831990d7e747ab">Why generate next intent before retrieval and verification in NEXT instead of linking the most semantically similar videos?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Anext-vlm">NEXT: Reasoning-Driven Video Recommendation via a Vision-Language Model</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Similarity describes content, not the next need. A VLM infers what follows, retrieval grounds it, and verification forms a directed edge. Expensive inference runs offline; positive engagement triggers confident edges online. The graph expresses possible continuation, not symmetric similarity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: After a coffee-machine unboxing, extraction instructions may be a better next step than another unboxing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24789">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.24789-next-vlm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7f831990d7e747ab">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:next-vlm" data-paper-title="NEXT: Reasoning-Driven Video Recommendation via a Vision-Language Model" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-7dcbd227aeffe137">How does NEXT&#x27;s intent–retrieve–verify chain improve reliability over asking a VLM to name the next video?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Anext-vlm">NEXT: Reasoning-Driven Video Recommendation via a Vision-Language Model</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Intent states the need, retrieval grounds it in the catalog, and verification checks fit, reducing invented titles. The stages can still inherit wrong intent or missed retrieval. A local proxy graph increment does not reproduce full NEXT-8B training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Infer &#x27;learn how to use it,&#x27; retrieve and verify a real tutorial; a bad initial intent can still steer the entire chain wrong.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24789">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.24789-next-vlm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7dcbd227aeffe137">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:next-vlm" data-paper-title="NEXT: Reasoning-Driven Video Recommendation via a Vision-Language Model" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f9e4c0fc5abbe8b3">Why inject NEXT NKG candidates additively only after positive engagement?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Anext-vlm">NEXT: Reasoning-Driven Video Recommendation via a Vision-Language Model</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Positive feedback triggers continuation, while additive candidates supplement production retrieval instead of replacing it with uncertain graph edges. The trigger must already be observed; deduplicate and enforce eligibility. A large single-seed proxy change applies to its fixed protocol only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Add tutorial candidates after a user likes an unboxing, not after a skip; retain other retrieval options.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24789">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.24789-next-vlm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f9e4c0fc5abbe8b3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:oneshot-index" data-paper-title="OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-oneshot-index-d86efe4f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-09ee1ff47d178754">Why make the index path part of OneShot rather than cluster after training?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aoneshot-index">OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta / Instagram</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Post-training clustering follows existing geometry and can disagree with ranking. Joint training uses behavior loss to shape buckets, then a strong scorer distinguishes retrieved items. Discrete routing and balancing can still reduce coverage and may not help at every scale.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Ranking can separate items with similar text but distinct buyers. A fixed bucket can hide the right item from even a good scorer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27475">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.27475-oneshot-index/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-09ee1ff47d178754">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:oneshot-index" data-paper-title="OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-43a83253198c0a11">How does OneShot train discrete hierarchical addresses on ranking rather than embedding-distance clusters?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aoneshot-index">OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta / Instagram</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Forward passes take discrete paths; straight-through gradients approximate ranking-loss feedback to assignment parameters. Global balancing avoids crowded paths, and neural scoring ranks retrieved candidates. Joint learning aligns objectives, but approximate gradients and balanced load do not guarantee relevance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Similar text with different audiences can be assigned to different paths by behavior; balancing can keep popular items from overloading one bucket.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:oneshot-index" data-paper-title="OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ae072d6a59aa6979">Why do OneShot path balancing and popularity penalties affect different objects?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aoneshot-index">OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta / Instagram</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Path balancing manages bucket load and resources. Popularity penalties alter recommendation preference. Balanced buckets may spread popular items without reducing their exposure, so measure index use and business distribution separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Ten popular items can fill ten distinct buckets and still all be recommended.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27475">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.27475-oneshot-index/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ae072d6a59aa6979">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:oneshot-index" data-paper-title="OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-713862f67a90446c">Why check OneShot&#x27;s straight-through forward and backward behavior separately?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aoneshot-index">OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta / Instagram</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Forward must choose a real discrete one-hot route; backward approximates with softmax gradients. Fully soft assignment is not discrete serving, while hard argmax may block gradients. Align path, item map, and scorer versions to verify ranking trains addresses.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Routing weights receive gradients, but one forward still chooses one prescribed path, not a mix of all buckets.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27475">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.27475-oneshot-index/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-713862f67a90446c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pair" data-paper-title="PAIR: Preference-Aligned Intent Retrieval for Premium People Recommendation at LinkedIn" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-pair-40d29d93" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-5a6b8f1b86d82b97">Why does PAIR model professional relevance as complementarity rather than mere similarity?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apair">PAIR: Preference-Aligned Intent Retrieval for Premium People Recommendation at LinkedIn</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · LinkedIn</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A member may need a recruiter, client, or different skill set. Shared profile encoding and history use clicked versus skipped members under the same exposure to learn such relationships. Complementarity remains scenario-dependent, not a rule to recommend dissimilar people.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: An engineer looking for work may need a recruiter; when looking for a technical peer, another engineer may be relevant.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与服务边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30941v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2610.30941-pair/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5a6b8f1b86d82b97">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pair" data-paper-title="PAIR: Preference-Aligned Intent Retrieval for Premium People Recommendation at LinkedIn" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-41753ca1acfbc839">Why isn&#x27;t PAIR&#x27;s multi-negative preference loss token-level DPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apair">PAIR: Preference-Aligned Intent Retrieval for Premium People Recommendation at LinkedIn</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · LinkedIn</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Clicked candidates, non-clicked candidates from the same exposure, and random members train profile and history encoders for complementary relevance. This is a multi-negative contrastive score objective with no token probability ratios, explicit reference, or KL term. The preference comes from exposure-conditioned supervision.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A job seeker selects a recruiter over a similar job seeker; compare candidate representations, not answer-token probabilities.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与服务边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30941v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2610.30941-pair/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-41753ca1acfbc839">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pair" data-paper-title="PAIR: Preference-Aligned Intent Retrieval for Premium People Recommendation at LinkedIn" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-f86c93423be74324">What difficulty do same-exposure non-clicks and random member negatives add in PAIR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apair">PAIR: Preference-Aligned Intent Retrieval for Premium People Recommendation at LinkedIn</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · LinkedIn</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Exposed non-clicks represent real competitors; random members offer broad, often easier contrast. The mix learns fine choice and global structure. Non-clicks can reflect position or opportunity, not true negatives. Preference does not imply token DPO or removal of exposure bias.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Two local recruiters create a fine comparison; a random unrelated student is easier and does not replace the exposed choice.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与服务边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30941v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2610.30941-pair/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f86c93423be74324">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pair" data-paper-title="PAIR: Preference-Aligned Intent Retrieval for Premium People Recommendation at LinkedIn" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f03a7c6d20c75741">How verify PAIR history positions, padding, and candidate identity without future clicks?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apair">PAIR: Preference-Aligned Intent Retrieval for Premium People Recommendation at LinkedIn</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · LinkedIn</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Use only pre-request events, ensure masked padding changes cannot affect scores, and align candidate profiles with labels. Position changes may affect results as designed. Gradient checks and CUDA smoke verify operators, not professional recommendation gains. Do not add a reference KL to the contrastive objective.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Perturbing masked history should not change a score; reading a future clicked candidate to improve prediction leaks the answer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与服务边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30941v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2610.30941-pair/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f03a7c6d20c75741">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:policy-facet" data-paper-title="Policy-Grounded Dynamic Facet Suggestions for Job Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-policy-facet-10555aa9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-1d64a12b7237f3f1">Are Policy Facet&#x27;s facets the same candidates as final products or documents?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apolicy-facet">Policy-Grounded Dynamic Facet Suggestions for Job Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · LinkedIn</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Facets are refinement options that alter later search or browsing; items satisfy the resulting request. A facet must meet taxonomy and usefulness requirements. A high-scoring item title does not automatically make a useful refinement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: &#x27;Family activities&#x27; narrows travel search; a specific museum ticket is a result.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16479">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.16479-policy-facet/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1d64a12b7237f3f1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:policy-facet" data-paper-title="Policy-Grounded Dynamic Facet Suggestions for Job Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-1a873ae567d00c7d">Why maintain a policy-controlled taxonomy before small-model retrieval and single-token scoring in Policy Facet?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apolicy-facet">Policy-Grounded Dynamic Facet Suggestions for Job Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · LinkedIn</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A curated set bounds themes, preventing arbitrary out-of-policy generation. Embeddings retrieve cheaply within it and a compact generator scores a token such as &#x27;Okay&#x27; conditioned on user and query. Caching and batching lower latency. High model probability does not complete policy enforcement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Choose a family travel facet from maintained destination and activity categories rather than inventing one live.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16479">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.16479-policy-facet/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1a873ae567d00c7d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:policy-facet" data-paper-title="Policy-Grounded Dynamic Facet Suggestions for Job Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4f7b6dbe5963d4ef">Why is an &#x27;Okay&#x27; token probability cheaper than generating full judgments?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apolicy-facet">Policy-Grounded Dynamic Facet Suggestions for Job Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · LinkedIn</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A bounded output gives a pointwise score without long decoding for every candidate; prefix caching and batching add reuse. It loses detailed reasoning and needs calibration. Scoring cannot recover facets missed in retrieval.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Read one probability for ten facets instead of generating ten long reviews, but an unretrieved option never gets scored.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16479">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.16479-policy-facet/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4f7b6dbe5963d4ef">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:policy-facet" data-paper-title="Policy-Grounded Dynamic Facet Suggestions for Job Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-eaf1989efcddb804">Why verify tokenizer and full conditioning prefix for Policy Facet&#x27;s &#x27;Okay&#x27; score?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apolicy-facet">Policy-Grounded Dynamic Facet Suggestions for Job Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · LinkedIn</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The word may tokenize differently across models. Read the designated output under the right user, query, and facet prefix. A hardcoded vocabulary ID can score another word after model changes; caches must not include another facet. Local proxy latency is not production evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: If &#x27;Okay&#x27; becomes two tokens, the old single ID may be wrong even though it returns a finite number.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankgraph2" data-paper-title="RankGraph-2: Lifecycle Co-Design for Billion-Node Graph Learning in Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-rankgraph2-ef314ec2" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-bbf469a8879df2f5">Why combine restart with multi-hop propagation in RankGraph-2 PPR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankgraph2">RankGraph-2: Lifecycle Co-Design for Billion-Node Graph Learning in Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Restart preserves seed personalization while corrected multi-hop edges expand beyond immediate neighbors. Popularity adjustments reduce mass concentration, but do not prove unbiased relations. Stale graphs and index compression can lose tail paths.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Photography links through lenses to tutorials; restarting avoids drifting entirely to site-wide hits.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18379">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2606.18379-rankgraph2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bbf469a8879df2f5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankgraph2" data-paper-title="RankGraph-2: Lifecycle Co-Design for Billion-Node Graph Learning in Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ac6d4c7748c03d76">Why correct popular edges before offline multi-hop PPR in RankGraph-2 rather than deploy a deeper online GNN?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankgraph2">RankGraph-2: Lifecycle Co-Design for Billion-Node Graph Learning in Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Multi-hop propagation finds indirect links but popular nodes absorb mass and online depth costs latency. Correct transitions and compute PPR offline, then compress serving via residuals and cluster indexing. Popularity correction does not eliminate all exposure bias, and the graph needs refreshes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A blockbuster can connect unrelated films. Reducing its incoming transition weight lets niche relations survive across hops.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18379">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2606.18379-rankgraph2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ac6d4c7748c03d76">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankgraph2" data-paper-title="RankGraph-2: Lifecycle Co-Design for Billion-Node Graph Learning in Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-8de9c180a87e7923">How do offline PPR plus a compressed index and online deep GNN trade cost for freshness?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankgraph2">RankGraph-2: Lifecycle Co-Design for Billion-Node Graph Learning in Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Offline computation amortizes hops and makes lookups light but may lag new edges or current intent. Online propagation is fresher but repeats work per request. PPR iteration convergence is not end-to-end throughput; the proxy is not a full production ablation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: New content with links today waits for the offline refresh, while online propagation can read it at greater serving cost.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18379">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2606.18379-rankgraph2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8de9c180a87e7923">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankgraph2" data-paper-title="RankGraph-2: Lifecycle Co-Design for Billion-Node Graph Learning in Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-e362d9fc430e281c">Why renormalize transitions after RankGraph-2 popularity correction before PPR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankgraph2">RankGraph-2: Lifecycle Co-Design for Billion-Node Graph Learning in Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Reweighting changes row sums. Renormalize to legal transitions or probability mass is spuriously lost or amplified. Check isolates and restart, and validate residual/cluster indexing separately. Designed debiasing does not prove all exposure bias is gone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A row sum falling to 0.4 would lose 60% of mass each hop without renormalization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18379">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2606.18379-rankgraph2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e362d9fc430e281c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rptune" data-paper-title="RPTune: Learned Context Curation for LLM Catalog Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-rptune-1e6a74b6" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-cfc59a331b753a91">What does RPTune pruning decide, and what does positioning decide?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arptune">RPTune: Learned Context Curation for LLM Catalog Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Pruning decides which catalog products enter the prompt; positioning sets the order of retained products. One changes the selectable set and the other changes context for reading the same set. Reordering cannot recover a dropped product.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Keep ten products out of a thousand, then reorder the ten. The second step cannot restore deleted items.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00964">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.00964-rptune/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cfc59a331b753a91">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rptune" data-paper-title="RPTune: Learned Context Curation for LLM Catalog Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-e2aa86945fffe4e8">Why place high-priority products in ascending order near the prompt end?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arptune">RPTune: Learned Context Curation for LLM Catalog Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Learned query–product scores determine what stays; positions near the response are a separate optimization. Post-training adapts to that catalog input. Local tests check arrangement, not a universal position preference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>With three slots, drop weak candidates, then place the best affordable product nearest the answer. Test selection and placement separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00964">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.00964-rptune/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e2aa86945fffe4e8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rptune" data-paper-title="RPTune: Learned Context Curation for LLM Catalog Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-51d8e0ae47576123">Are RPTune&#x27;s product scoring and prompt ordering both just vector top-k?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arptune">RPTune: Learned Context Curation for LLM Catalog Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Scoring adds learned query and product adjustments to the semantic dot product. After top-k, a prescribed positioning rule orders the LLM input. Vector top-k alone has neither learned adjustment nor that order. Ablate set selection and positioning separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two methods can keep the same ten products in different orders, or choose different sets under the same ordering rule.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00964">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.00964-rptune/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-51d8e0ae47576123">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rptune" data-paper-title="RPTune: Learned Context Curation for LLM Catalog Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-825fb1cf921dcc1c">Why does RPTune sort retained top-k products in ascending score order?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arptune">RPTune: Learned Context Curation for LLM Catalog Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Its layout puts high scores near the end. After retention, sort ascending rather than defaulting to descending. The local rank/prune/position kernel does not call the paper&#x27;s LLM or run full post-training, so it cannot report full catalog-search gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Placing the top-scoring item first reverses the intended end preference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00964">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.00964-rptune/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-825fb1cf921dcc1c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:setmir" data-paper-title="SetMIR: Multi-Interest Retrieval as Set Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-setmir-231692c0" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-1dbb7554298c2ace">Is a SetMIR query a user-entered search string?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asetmir">SetMIR: Multi-Interest Retrieval as Set Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It is a generated interest vector or slot for ANN. Multiple slots capture possible interests; serving rules decide which activate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Opening recommendations can produce sports and photography vectors without a typed query.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30251">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.30251-setmir/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1dbb7554298c2ace">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:setmir" data-paper-title="SetMIR: Multi-Interest Retrieval as Set Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-92167d9dee9cf98d">Why use one-to-one matching in training and presence/NMS in serving?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asetmir">SetMIR: Multi-Interest Retrieval as Set Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Matching prevents training collapse onto one positive. Presence activates relevant slots per request; NMS removes redundant retrieval calls. These solve different problems.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Activate photography and camping, then suppress two nearly identical camera queries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30251">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.30251-setmir/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-92167d9dee9cf98d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:setmir" data-paper-title="SetMIR: Multi-Interest Retrieval as Set Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-37ab5a0653ba7420">How does one-to-one set matching differ from independent slot choices?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asetmir">SetMIR: Multi-Interest Retrieval as Set Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Joint assignment limits slots from repeatedly explaining one easy positive. It needs reliable target sets; unique assignments do not prove complete interest discovery.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Assign slots to sports and photography rather than both greedily choosing sports.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30251">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.30251-setmir/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-37ab5a0653ba7420">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:setmir" data-paper-title="SetMIR: Multi-Interest Retrieval as Set Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-9c478711239026dd">Which SetMIR queries actually dispatch ANN?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asetmir">SetMIR: Multi-Interest Retrieval as Set Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Only those passing presence and surviving query NMS. The public CPU path does not reproduce private histories, production Transformer, or ANN dispatch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Ten available slots need not make ten calls.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30251">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.30251-setmir/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9c478711239026dd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:snap-dpa-relevance" data-paper-title="LLM-based User-Product Relevance Evaluation for Dynamic Product Advertising" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-snap-dpa-relevance-9f0c9ccb" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-9395ea2a026ef61e">Why compress intent rather than equate clicks with Snap DPA relevance?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asnap-dpa-relevance">LLM-based User-Product Relevance Evaluation for Dynamic Product Advertising</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Clicks are sparse and exposure-biased. Group recent behavior by SID and event type, then apply business-aligned relevance criteria. This is a separate demand metric, not renamed CTR.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Repeated recent cart additions can be stronger intent evidence than one exposure.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14550">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.14550-snap-dpa-relevance/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9395ea2a026ef61e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:snap-dpa-relevance" data-paper-title="LLM-based User-Product Relevance Evaluation for Dynamic Product Advertising" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-9d5c6706cb902a75">Why distinguish MicroRel and MacroRel and vet criteria first?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asnap-dpa-relevance">LLM-based User-Product Relevance Evaluation for Dynamic Product Advertising</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Compressed history supplies intent; a criteria-trained detector judges candidates. Pair-level and user-level averages answer different questions, but neither repairs wrong relevance judgments. Private review and commercial model workflows are not reproduced.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>With 100 and ten candidates, user one weighs ten times as much in micro but equally in macro.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14550">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.14550-snap-dpa-relevance/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9d5c6706cb902a75">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:snap-dpa-relevance" data-paper-title="LLM-based User-Product Relevance Evaluation for Dynamic Product Advertising" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-59a1b674f56a0a46">Why can MicroRel and MacroRel disagree?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asnap-dpa-relevance">LLM-based User-Product Relevance Evaluation for Dynamic Product Advertising</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Micro averages user–candidate pairs, while macro weights users equally. Users with many candidates dominate micro more. Report both rather than cherry-pick.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Active users with many candidates affect micro disproportionately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14550">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.14550-snap-dpa-relevance/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-59a1b674f56a0a46">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:snap-dpa-relevance" data-paper-title="LLM-based User-Product Relevance Evaluation for Dynamic Product Advertising" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ec1c2b80c0f2fa30">Can gold relevance labels stand in for detector predictions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asnap-dpa-relevance">LLM-based User-Product Relevance Evaluation for Dynamic Product Advertising</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Train a real detector on discovered, human-reviewed business criteria and evaluate independently. Rule discovery has bootstrap and per-class F1 requirements; coverage review cannot be skipped.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Copying gold computes a score without learning relevance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14550">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.14550-snap-dpa-relevance/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ec1c2b80c0f2fa30">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:spear" data-paper-title="SPEAR: Selection-aware Personalized End-to-end Adaptive Rewriting and Retrieval for Community Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-spear-7c6c6f8e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d1837bff0f6de91d">Why preserve original-query retrieval semantics in SPEAR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aspear">SPEAR: Selection-aware Personalized End-to-end Adaptive Rewriting and Retrieval for Community Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Dewu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Generic rewrites can exploit high path scores while drifting. Separate embeddings and gradients preserve retrieval; confidence times item relevance limits amplification.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A running-shoe query should not rank unrelated sports items by popularity alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01738">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.01738-spear/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d1837bff0f6de91d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:spear" data-paper-title="SPEAR: Selection-aware Personalized End-to-end Adaptive Rewriting and Retrieval for Community Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-df3bee67260ec58e">Why multiply rewrite confidence and item relevance while separating embedding gradients?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aspear">SPEAR: Selection-aware Personalized End-to-end Adaptive Rewriting and Retrieval for Community Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Dewu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Generic rewrites can win with misleading path scores. Product gating needs both trust and relevance; gradient isolation protects original retrieval semantics from ranking optimization. Request-level calibration does not guarantee correct confidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Replacing waterproof hiking boots with “popular products” should lose confidence despite high clicks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01738">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.01738-spear/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-df3bee67260ec58e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:spear" data-paper-title="SPEAR: Selection-aware Personalized End-to-end Adaptive Rewriting and Retrieval for Community Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a7ebe4a3068ccbd8">How does a multiplicative gate differ from adding confidence and relevance?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aspear">SPEAR: Selection-aware Personalized End-to-end Adaptive Rewriting and Retrieval for Community Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Dewu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Both inputs must support the product; addition can let one high score compensate for the other. Dynamic selection also calibrates request-level scale and bias.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A confident rewrite cannot rescue an irrelevant item by confidence alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01738">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.01738-spear/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a7ebe4a3068ccbd8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:spear" data-paper-title="SPEAR: Selection-aware Personalized End-to-end Adaptive Rewriting and Retrieval for Community Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-38144047487ed4ce">Does the local two-path SPEAR proxy generate real rewrites?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aspear">SPEAR: Selection-aware Personalized End-to-end Adaptive Rewriting and Retrieval for Community Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Dewu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. MovieLens content proxies products/posts without private sessions or a production generator. Keep original scores and isolate embedding gradients; do not pick rewrites on test.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Scoring a handwritten rewrite does not show generation.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:toolrec" data-paper-title="ToolRec: Calibrated Preference Alignment for Query Recommendation in On-Device Assistants" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-toolrec-2caef440" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-25a7db10326f0f87">Does tool frequency mean more calls are better?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atoolrec">ToolRec: Calibrated Preference Alignment for Query Recommendation in On-Device Assistants</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huazhong University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It is a system calibration signal, not user relevance or successful-call quality. Evaluate use distribution and utility separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Raising an uncommon tool&#x27;s rate does not make it relevant to unrelated questions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08466">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2606.08466-toolrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-25a7db10326f0f87">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:toolrec" data-paper-title="ToolRec: Calibrated Preference Alignment for Query Recommendation in On-Device Assistants" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-b4bbc0c6ac0744e7">Why calibrate user preference and tool frequency rather than reward triggers alone?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atoolrec">ToolRec: Calibrated Preference Alignment for Query Recommendation in On-Device Assistants</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huazhong University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Trigger-only rewards overcall irrelevant tools; user-only optimization may ignore supply/use imbalance. Dynamic weights balance both, but frequency is governance, not quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Live flight questions may need a tool, whereas definitions need not call it to boost frequency.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08466">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2606.08466-toolrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b4bbc0c6ac0744e7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:toolrec" data-paper-title="ToolRec: Calibrated Preference Alignment for Query Recommendation in On-Device Assistants" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b00694e9f0f66520">How do dynamic frequency weights differ from a fixed positive/negative ratio?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atoolrec">ToolRec: Calibrated Preference Alignment for Query Recommendation in On-Device Assistants</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huazhong University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Dynamic weights follow tool-use statistics; fixed ratios do not. Frequency is not utility, so do not trade relevance away and report only triggers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A low-use tool can get more opportunities only where appropriate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08466">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2606.08466-toolrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b00694e9f0f66520">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:toolrec" data-paper-title="ToolRec: Calibrated Preference Alignment for Query Recommendation in On-Device Assistants" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-6d1486b37d004bc3">Does local ToolRec execute real tools?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atoolrec">ToolRec: Calibrated Preference Alignment for Query Recommendation in On-Device Assistants</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huazhong University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. MovieLens tests calibration/scoring without private sessions or tool calls. Use versioned training-window frequencies, not future test rates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Movie genre counts are not API cost or service load.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08466">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2606.08466-toolrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6d1486b37d004bc3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:transretrieval" data-paper-title="TransRetrieval: Scaling Up Transformer-Based Retrieval for Industrial Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-transretrieval-4252b15a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-74ee6b5fb450fd19">Why compress source history and target tokens?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atransretrieval">TransRetrieval: Scaling Up Transformer-Based Retrieval for Industrial Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Renmin University of China / Taobao &amp; Tmall Group, Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Source noise and many target tokens both raise cross-attention cost. Norm-aware pooling and target compression act at different ends; domain embeddings limit confusion. Compression loses detail.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Summarize source behavior and combine target fields before interaction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25528">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.25528-transretrieval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-74ee6b5fb450fd19">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:transretrieval" data-paper-title="TransRetrieval: Scaling Up Transformer-Based Retrieval for Industrial Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-246f8113bd997f04">Why norm-pool source history, compress target tokens, and add domain positions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atransretrieval">TransRetrieval: Scaling Up Transformer-Based Retrieval for Industrial Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Renmin University of China / Taobao &amp; Tmall Group, Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Norm weighting selects among noisy source events; target compression reduces cross-domain compute, while position/domain identity separates business meanings. Norm is not guaranteed relevant and compression can lose target detail.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Mark article saves and product purchases as different while compressing both sides for ad retrieval.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25528">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.25528-transretrieval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-246f8113bd997f04">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:transretrieval" data-paper-title="TransRetrieval: Scaling Up Transformer-Based Retrieval for Industrial Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-0be0037018c4d9ac">How does norm weighting differ from averaging source tokens?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atransretrieval">TransRetrieval: Scaling Up Transformer-Based Retrieval for Industrial Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Renmin University of China / Taobao &amp; Tmall Group, Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Larger norms get more weight, whereas mean is uniform. Norm is a proxy, not causal importance. Domain position encoding is not one shared constant.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A high-amplitude noisy feature may receive too much influence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25528">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.25528-transretrieval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0be0037018c4d9ac">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:transretrieval" data-paper-title="TransRetrieval: Scaling Up Transformer-Based Retrieval for Industrial Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-21beb67cd46b2b17">Does 85% fewer target FLOPs imply equal end-to-end latency savings?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atransretrieval">TransRetrieval: Scaling Up Transformer-Based Retrieval for Industrial Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Renmin University of China / Taobao &amp; Tmall Group, Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Structural counts omit memory movement and other service stages. No original 40B interactions, large ads catalog, or ANN are reproduced.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Preprocessing or retrieval can dominate even if attention arithmetic falls.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25528">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.25528-transretrieval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-21beb67cd46b2b17">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:youtube-dnn" data-paper-title="Deep Neural Networks for YouTube Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
